patch.objective: Know how the law reaches nurses: civil malpractice claims, failure to obtain consent as negligence, and Good Samaritan protection

sources.cite: AACN. The Essentials: Core Competencies for Professional Nursing Education (2026 edition, announced April 2026)
sources.note: Relayed from the BSN-RN course's earlier cases (read 2026-11-11, primary web page), not re-read for this band: the course's domains follow the Essentials; the domain placement is the course catalog's.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case preop-consent-after-opioid, not re-read for this band; its note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-RN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: the objective titles are the course's own, built from this test plan's client needs categories.

sources.cite: OpenStax, Fundamentals of Nursing (2024), section 16.3 (Rice University, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case preop-consent-after-opioid, not re-read for this band; its note: Relayed from the NCLEX course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/nursing.ts, accessed 2026-11-02), not re-read: the nurse's part in informed consent (signer of legal age, competent, acting voluntarily; escalate when the client does not understand), and that a nurse who knows consent was not properly obtained and does not tell the provider or a supervisor can be held liable, and treating without consent may be battery.

sources.cite: Open RN. Nursing Fundamentals, 1.6 Legal and Ethical Considerations (Chippewa Valley Technical College, CC BY 4.0)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case preop-consent-after-opioid, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes: informed consent covers 'its benefits, risks, potential complications; reasonable alternatives to treatment; and the right to withdraw consent', as 'written consent voluntarily signed by a client who is competent'; 'The nurse often signs as a witness to the client's signature on the form'; 'it is not the nurse's responsibility or role to provide information'; if the client 'expresses questions, concerns, or lack of understanding', 'notify the provider and advocate for further discussion before signing the form'. The page does not address sedating drugs; the unit's policy covers them.

sources.cite: Open RN. Nursing Management and Professional Concepts, 5.6 Other Legal Issues (Ernstmeyer and Christman, eds.; LibreTexts copy, modified 2023-02-03; CC BY 4.0)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case preop-consent-after-opioid, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch with quotes: 'physicians have the responsibility to provide information and obtain informed consent related to medical procedures'; nurses 'verify the presence of a valid, signed informed consent before the procedure is performed'; when the client does not seem to understand, 'request the provider return to clarify unclear information with the client'; 'It is outside the scope of practice for nurses to formally assess capacity'.
